OTOS Continuity™ · a private briefing

Treat the driver upstream,watch the cost chain collapse downstream.

As we both know and understand, there is rarely a single root cause of addiction. It grows out of a mix of trauma, mental health, genes and environment, and it is now widely seen as a complex condition of the brain, not a lack of willpower. But, as I mentioned in our meeting, there is something I believe — and, with support, can prove — is being missed.

For a significant, high-cost, identifiable group of adults — and for me, until mine was treated — untreated ADHD is driving relapse by recycling and fanning the fire of the addiction, regardless of origin. The chaos, crises and costs are just what arrives in view.

My simple but complicated idea is to intervene way earlier, then copy my journey, corrected. It is an intervention that gets the driver found and treated far earlier. Continuity is the non-clinical layer that holds a person in the days between the services already treating them — and it carries the whole thing: from the intervention through to a brain that is finally treated properly and can find its own way Out The Other Side. The way I did, without what it cost me to get there.

This is a plan to stop what happened to me happening to the next person, and I believe it takes a great deal of money out of this system. The method is the same for any complex cohort: identify the person far earlier, upstream; hold them through every handoff; and act before repeat chaos becomes repeat crisis, consequence and cost.

The evidence behind the savings

Why the underlying driver is worth addressing.

None of this is mine and none of it is a finding. It is the published base any serious look at this would start from — and it is as far as reading gets you. What none of it does is tell you whether the pattern is here, in Cambridgeshire, in your cohort. That is the gap.

74%

starting addiction treatment have mental-health needs

Gov UK NDTMS

adults seeking treatment for substance use also have ADHD — 3,578 patients, 47 sites, 10 countries. The UK was not one of them.

International Collaboration on ADHD and Substance Abuse (ICASA) · European Addiction Research 2020

The national annual burden.

£17bn

avoidable annual cost of untreated ADHD

NHS England ADHD Taskforce 2025

The system already spends heavily — but often too late. OTOS asks to test a lighter, earlier intervention around a cohort that is already costing too much to lose.

What the national guidance says

  • NICE NG87, recommendation 1.2.1 names people with a history of substance misuse, and adults with a mental health condition, among the groups who may have increased ADHD prevalence. Recommendation 1.4.3 uses the words substance misuse and self-medication.
  • RCPsych CR235, s11.1 records that substance misuse “may be twice as common among individuals with ADHD as in the general population and tends to begin earlier”, and that individuals with untreated ADHD “may also describe self-medicating with illicit substances”.
  • Neither body says what to do about the overlap inside an addiction service. That is the question this asks.

And the two things CR235 also says, which I would rather raise myself: it recommends stabilising substance misuse first, and it says stimulants are not routinely recommended in chaotic misuse. Those are real constraints on any priority-review route, and they belong in the design, not in the small print.

What the £4,950 actually buys

This is the evidence base, and working through it properly is the job. The national datasets. Your own commissioned documents. Read against one question, systematically, and reported back in a form you could take to a decision.

I have read enough to be confident the question is real. I have deliberately not put my working in front of you, because the working is the thing I am asking you to fund. What I am offering is not a conclusion I already hold. It is the capability to establish one, here, defensibly, for less than the cost of a single residential placement.

08

The cost that is already being paid

Nobody is being asked for new money. The money is already leaving.

The national anchor is not mine and does not need to be. The independent ADHD Taskforce, reporting to NHS England, put the economic cost to individuals and government at "at least £17 billion" a year and named the drivers: unemployment, crime, substance misuse.

The sentence is worth reading whole, because of the order it is written in. NHS England’s own independent taskforce, in the Abbreviated Summary of Part 1 and again in Part 2, identical wording in both:

ADHD, when unsupported, is a potent route into educational failure, long-term unemployment, crime, substance misuse, suicide, mental and physical illness. Economic costs to individuals and the government of at least £17 billion are avoidable as, when appropriately supported, people with ADHD can thrive and fully engage in a working life.

That list is incredibly close to what happened to me. I did not write it. It is NHS England’s, in their own report.

Where the £17 billion comes from, and what the Taskforce says about it

Part 1, §3, “What are the costs of not treating ADHD?”: using Danish patient registry data, the cost difference between adults with ADHD and their same-sex siblings was approximately £17,000 more per adult with ADHD per year, and the UK estimate of £17 billion is that figure extrapolated at a prevalence of 2.5%. The underlying study is cited in the report as European Psychiatry (2019) 61:41–48.

And on the same page the Taskforce says this: “No published papers on the contemporary costs of untreated ADHD in the UK exist yet.”

It is a Danish-derived extrapolation and the report says so itself. On the only published estimate available is a more honest sentence than a bare number, and it is the one I will keep using.

Report of the independent ADHD Taskforce, NHS England — Part 1 published 20 June 2025, Part 2 published 6 November 2025.

The same report gives the per-person figure I now use instead: adults with ADHD cost approximately £17,000 more per adult per year in public spending than their same-sex siblings. Danish registry data, sibling-controlled — which is methodologically stronger than anything my own model had.

Where that money goes is not new to you

A&E, ambulance, acute beds. Mental-health crisis care and admissions. Drug and alcohol treatment and repeat detox. GP, housing. None of that is a projection. It is this year's spend, on people your services already know by name, and it recurs because the driver underneath was never treated.

If CGL had just known I was in and out of A&E and waiting on the ADHD medication-review list, I could have avoided so much pain and loss — and the system wouldn’t have spent so much.

Nothing in that sentence asks for a new service. Two services were already treating me. Neither could see what the other could see.

I had the luck, the fight and the financial support to get out. My parents still pick up the bill for my private ADHD care, and that bill is still part of the ripple cost. I know there are people in the services you commission right now who cannot do what I did. They don’t have the resources, the language, the luck or the fight left in them.

I am not adding a number of my own on top of that. Every local figure on the next page is built from a published denominator and a labelled assumption, and it is shown with its working so you can disagree with any single step.

And one part of that spend you know better than I do. NICE names it directly: adults with a mental health condition, and people with a history of substance misuse, are both listed among the groups who may have increased prevalence of ADHD — NG87, recommendation 1.2.1.

The honest version of this page

An earlier version of this briefing carried a tiered "full ripple" cost model of my own — direct, family and system-wide, stacked into a headline per-person figure. I have taken it out.

I traced it this week and it did not survive. It had no primary source. Its stated authority was my own model citing itself. And it had been built two incompatible ways in two different files. It was the most persuasive page in the document and it was the least defensible, so it is gone, and I would rather you heard that from me than found it yourself.

What replaces it is smaller, and real.

  • How to read the local number — and why I am not giving you a headline

A defensible local number needs three things: a published denominator, a prevalence figure for this specific overlap, and an effect assumption grounded in something other than hope. Cambridgeshire has the first. It does not have the other two, and nor does anyone else. Establishing them here, against your own data, is what the report is for. I am not printing a headline saving built on numbers I would have to invent — that is the thing that gets a briefing thrown out, and it is also the work I am asking you to commission rather than pretending I have already done.

The three caveats on the £17,000, stated before you ask

It is Danish registry data, not UK.

It is a sibling comparison, not a whole-system cost.

It describes adults with ADHD — not adults with ADHD and addiction. Which means the cohort I am describing would plausibly cost more, not less. That is an argument to make. It is not a number I will assert.

What the pre-pilot is for is to replace both assumptions with something locally validated, so the next version of this page has a number neither of us has to caveat.

And the saving is only half of it

The system does not come out level. It comes out up.

Medicating this cohort properly doesn’t just save the system money. It is a double win: the system ends up up, not down, and not break-even.

Every cost model on this page counts one side of the ledger only — spend avoided. It does not count what a treated adult puts back: work, tax, a household that is not being held up by the state. Both sides move in the same direction, which is why the avoided-cost figure is the conservative one.

The case in one line

The cost does not disappear. It moves to a worse budget line.

Unaddressed, this cohort does not stop costing money — it costs more, later, across A&E, crisis care and repeat treatment. We are already paying. The only question is whether we pay upstream, once, or downstream, forever.

Every figure, its source, and what it is not.

Nothing on this page is an OTOS result. Everything is either a published figure with its source named, or a number you set yourself. Here is each one.

4,690 — the pool: every adult in structured addiction treatment, not the cohort

NDTMS 2024/25. Cambridgeshire 2,980 plus Peterborough 1,710. A published count, not an estimate.

£17,000 — additional public cost per adult with ADHD, per year

The slider — and why there is only one

The slider is the group you choose from that pool. There is no verified prevalence figure for ADHD within UK addiction-treatment populations. None. So rather than multiply one published figure by two assumptions I would have to invent, the model does a single multiplication and lets you supply the only uncertain term. The result is arithmetic, not a forecast, not a projection, and not a claim about what Cambridgeshire would save. It shows the size of the spend already attached to a group that size. How much of it could move is exactly what nobody yet knows.

What Continuity is

One layer, around the person, between the services already treating them.

No one owns the risk in the gap, so we decided to occupy it.

OTOS asks no organisation to take on that risk, that liability or that caseload. It fills the time — continuity, connection, communication, education, learning — so the gap stops belonging to nobody.

The cost case

A cost-redirection opportunity, hiding in current spend.

This is not a new cost. It is a smarter use of money the system is already spending — reactively, repeatedly, across budget lines that never speak to each other.

The savings land across several budget lines at once — which is exactly why no single budget holder has ever had a reason to fund the fix.

OTOS Continuity is infrastructure with a bounded pre-pilot, including intervention, for adults cycling through addiction and crisis, where unresolved ADHD may be the underlying driver of repeat demand. The whole case rests on one idea you'll recognise from your own data: the cost doesn't disappear — it moves to a different budget line.

The question underneath it: whether earlier intervention could take substantial recurring cost out of the system and reduce relapse sharply, at the same time.
